en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Great Noble Counsel:
A Discourse by the Wise.
The Sage has abandoned the great burden,
the hindrances, and craving;
he is liberated, liberated, and beautiful to behold.
I pay homage to the most excellent, supreme Bodhi.
By the Sage, the elephant among sages,
those who had gone forth as wicked were conquered.
Just as there are various false doctrines,
such as those of Pūraṇa and others,
so too are the teachings of the Tathāgata.
They should master the worldly conventions;
by applying themselves with diligence,
the wise shall overcome those who act against their own welfare.
In this world, the essence for living beings is good conduct,
friends, teachers, and kinsmen;
one who possesses moral discipline, is wise, and is competent—
The learned one, seeing the goal,
having fashioned the gold of the Teacher’s sūtras into the form of a sword, [attained] the state of a poet-artisan.
Creating here the *Gajjapajjā* and other poetic ornaments,
making it delightful to the mind—
this is the work of one whose knowledge is clear.
The wise man does not seek his own benefit therein;
for the radiance of wine is like a mirror,
yet no reflection of the Great Fish (Makara) is seen within it.
Though possessing great majesty,
he does not desire this majesty; he makes the earth soft,
and he brings water to soften it.
One should speak kindly even to a harsh person.
One conquers an enemy through gentleness;
one conquers the cruel through gentleness.
Nothing is accomplished by means of gentleness;
one should conquer through gentleness with effort.
Sandalwood is cool in the world.
Then, like the moon, it is cool;
from that which is as cool as sandalwood and the moon,
comes speech that is well-spoken by the virtuous.
Even a small word uttered at the right time may be well-spoken;
even a meager morsel of food [is welcome] to one who is hungry.
The discourse should be full of flavor.
Even though teachers may have many words,
those who speak much are not to be respected.
The water of the river is indifferent,
neither helpful nor harmful, and is not seen [as a fixed entity];
it is like the spreading tree of saṃsāra.
There are only two things that yield the fruit of the deathless:
the essence of well-spoken words and association with the virtuous.
The stone parasol is heavy;
after that, Devānañciya;
after that, the instruction of the elders.
Then there is the teaching of the Buddha;
it is very light compared to [worldly] weights in this world.
Therefore, one who is by nature fickle—
Then, from that [teacher], one who teaches according to that [Dharma] becomes a practitioner who grasps the Dharma.
Alas, as I go, it is diminishing.
The life of beings here is short;
therefore, do not be negligent,
but proceed in the teaching of the Conqueror.
For the praise of the wise,
punishment is inflicted by the fool;
yet the wise man is [praised] by the wise alone.
He who is praised is indeed well-praised.
Among hundreds a hero is born,
and among thousands a wise man.
It has been said that among hundreds of thousands,
there may or may not be one who gives;
yet such a person attains both sovereignty over the earth and wisdom.
A king is honored only in his own country, but the Buddha is honored everywhere.
Never is there one equal to him.
What is too heavy for those who are capable?
What distance is too far for those engaged in business?
What is a foreign land for those possessed of knowledge?
Even Mount Meru, the ocean,
the elephant Nalagiri, and Mount Malaya—
do these not belong to you who speak kindly?
Even those who abandon their own boundaries when the world is being destroyed, preserve the ancient boundaries that have come down to them.
It is said that the oceans, though they may perish even at the end of an eon,
do not wish to overstep their boundaries.
The virtuous are long-lived and bring happiness to all beings;
but the non-virtuous are likewise for all.
There is no doubt that this is the cause of suffering.
When virtuous people are preeminent,
all people indeed become virtuous.
When a single sāragandha tree has been born, all trees become fragrant;
if by oneself alone...
All great people follow the discipline established by Vinata;
what wise person would destroy it?
Between the body and its qualities,
there is an exceedingly vast and ultimate difference;
the body perishes in an instant, but the qualities endure.
Virtues endure for as long as the aeon.
If the eternal were [united] with the impermanent,
and the stainless with the bearer of stain;
If one were to obtain through the body that which has not been obtained, what would it be?
Would it be nothing at all? [It is] of the Dhamma, of the goal, of desire, and of liberation.
Life is the cause of success;
if it is destroyed, what is not destroyed?
If it is protected, what is not protected?
The self is the kinsman of a person;
the self alone is the enemy of living beings;
the self alone is the constant relative.
The self alone is one's certain enemy.
That which is the guarding of what has been surrendered through the relinquishing of the self—
Only the virtuous act thus;
this is not considered the way of those possessed of moral discipline.
Grass, earth, and water—
And fourthly, excellence of speech;
for these [qualities] in the house of the virtuous are never cut off at any time.
The river drinks the water;
the tree eats the fruit;
the cloud [provides for] the crop nowhere at all.
The wealth of the virtuous is for the sake of others;
the minds of the virtuous do not undergo transformation through harsh words.
It is not possible to heat the waters of the ocean even with grass-torches; likewise,
the mind’s present greatness—
It becomes as delicate as a blue lotus,
yet it pierces through a great rock,
rough with its mass of stones.
Having attained great purpose and even the perfection of true knowledge,
one should wander without pride or arrogance.
He is called wise:
he does not crave for what cannot be obtained,
nor does he grieve over what is lost.
They fall away and become bewildered;
therefore, one who understands even a single word at a difficult point is truly wise.
A wise person should not despise him;
for what is a mere bamboo stump compared to the sun that illuminates the three great worlds?
There is no one who is exempt from both virtues and faults,
even for the delicate lotus.
The reeds are rough and coarse;
though they possess very large blades,
they are full of holes.
The four doubts that torment those afflicted by greed and delusion,
as well as seeing faults even in that which possesses virtues—
The world does not see the mark on the moon, even though it exists, because the speaker speaks only of its qualities.
One who seeks the meaning through learning should listen with skill,
having investigated thoroughly,
like rice that has been cooked in a frying pan.
Even so may the vessel be.
Virtues act as messengers for the virtuous,
even though they dwell far away.
The bees go of their own accord to the scent of the ketaki flower;
so too does the wise man, endowed with learning.
Wherever it may be, according to these reasons,
that place must be gone to with great effort by one who seeks the Teaching.
One should thoroughly master all that has been heard—
the inferior, the superior, and the middling—
and one should understand the meaning of it all.
One should not employ everything;
there is such a time when learning brings about what is beneficial.
Thita remained for a long time in the water;
Sakkhara was born nearby;
Dabba was born close to the water's edge.
Those situated far away take up wealth from a mountain rich in gems,
even across all intervening times.
Just as non-Aryans do not stand near [the wise],
so fools do not stand near those who are learned;
they are like deer [frightened] by gold.
What is the use of learning for fools who, though virtuous, act unrighteously toward those who are immoral?
In the sense of being heard,
the fool is not virtuous at all;
in the sense of a hollow, he is like honey.
Why does the neem tree become sweet?
Even once, a wise person of firm mind forms a connection with it.
For one's own sake and for the sake of others,
may I attain the bliss that culminates in Nibbāna;
like a swan in the midst of crows.
A lion does not shine among sheep;
a thoroughbred horse does not shine among donkeys;
nor does a wise man shine among fools.
Though surrounded by the wicked,
the virtuous man remains unassociated with them;
even when crowded by a great multitude of the base, he stays aloof.
One might go here with a madman,
or to a well dug on a riverbank,
or to a fire-drill and its handle.
"There is nothing new in the world," so it is said;
likewise, there is no new word in the mouth.
The wise are those who have accumulated what they have heard.
Though questioned, she remained silent;
though well-spoken to by Puṇṇā,
she was like a bell that has not been struck.
The wise man is like a drum when unasked,
but becomes like rainclouds when questioned;
the fool, however, is like both when asked and when unasked.
He always boasts much.
Yet he is one whose virtues are perfected as his adornment,
bringing benefit to all beings.
One should not practice for the sake of another;
how could such a person be wise?
A steadfast person should practice for the sake of both self and others.
If one is unable to act for oneself,
one should at least distance oneself from evil deeds. And if one is unable even to do that, one should at least refrain from them.
A wise person, having committed no fault, should not act [wrongly] even toward a king who is foolish or intoxicated,
nor even toward one's own teachers, mother, or father.
In the Saṅgha and toward one’s elder brother,
loss of wealth, mental anguish,
and misconduct within the household.
A wise person should not display deceit or contempt;
[he should treat] the gift of another like his own mother.
The world is greedy for another's property;
he who sees all beings as himself— only he truly sees.
One who is deaf-mute regarding the slandering of others,
one who does not look at the faults of others,
and one who is lame toward other women.
In an evil age,
one who lacks consciousness hears everything with the ear and sees everything with the eye.
The wise person does not deserve to accumulate everything that has not been seen or heard;
it is like a blind man [trying to gather] what is before his eyes.
Like a deaf person hearing,
like a mute possessing wisdom,
like a strong man appearing weak;
But when a need has arisen,
one might lie down like one who is dead.
Having avoided evil friends, [one should seek the good].
One should attend upon the Supreme Person;
one should abide by his instruction,
aspiring for unshakable happiness.
Learning increases through hearing;
hearing increases wisdom;
through wisdom one understands the true goal.
A well-known purpose brings happiness;
it is a ground for joy and a source of praise and bliss.
One who bears the yoke of humanity develops the fruit of its benefits;
[avoiding] what is too cold and what is too hot.
"This is too much," they say;
thus, for those who are negligent in their work,
the moments pass away for the young man.
And he who, performing his duties as a man, regards cold and heat as mere grass—
Thus, happiness does not abandon him.
People avoid from afar a man who seeks to acquire fame and gain.
Therefore, having avoided those [wrong paths],
the wise person should seek that path.
They go astray by deviating from the instruction.
The lions, the true men,
and the elephants meet their end right there;
the crows, the base men, and the deer perish elsewhere.
In whatever place there is no assembly,
no mother, no kinsmen,
and no one who has attained true knowledge—
One does not dwell in the rains there.
These people are wealthy, accountants, kings,
rivers, and physicians.
Where the five do not exist,
there one does not dwell under their sway;
for food is the end of fear.
Death is the fear of mortals;
for all, the highest fear is the contempt of others.
Where there may be non-honoring,
the slighting of the peaceful ones,
and even the honoring of the base—
One should not dwell where the indolent and the skillful,
the brave and the cowardly, are all equally honored.
No rain falls there; who would cause such distinction?
Dwelling in confinement is suffering.
In a place crowded with impurity,
then among those who are dear to the flesh,
and then among those who are ungrateful.
One should give up five hundred golden coins for a single elephant,
a hundred horses for a single elephant,
and a thousand [coins] for a single elephant.
One should abandon the wicked through non-generosity;
one should abandon an individual for the sake of a family; one should abandon a family for the sake of a village.
A village for the sake of a district;
the earth would abandon itself for its own sake.
One might stand on one leg, yet...
The wise man stands alone;
he does not praise the doctrines of others,
nor does he abandon his own traditional path.
Those who have fallen from their station do not shine;
the teeth and hair are but objects for consumption.
Having understood this, the wise one—
The crafty do not abandon quickly;
one may abandon wealth for the sake of a superior limb,
and abandon a limb while protecting one's life.
A person who keeps the Dhamma in mind would give up even a limb, wealth, and life itself;
one's ear is for hearing the Dhamma, not for earrings.
The hand of the Supreme Person shines through generosity,
not by a bracelet; his body radiates through service to others, not by sandalwood paste.
Through investigation into the duration of the world-system,
the time of the wise passes in discourse that dispels confusion.
Through the misfortune of the wicked,
through sleep, or through quarrels—
there are thousands of occasions for sorrow.
And hundreds of occasions for fear will manifest day after day for the fool,
but not for the wise man.
The very tall one is greatly deluded,
while the medium one is discerning;
having placed Vāsudeva at their head, they [depart].
All dwarfs are crooked;
the fool who praises only himself does not shine in the world.
Even when hidden in a well,
the one who has mastered the knowledge shines forth;
the Teacher’s weapon is the taming of the intoxicated.
It produces intoxication for the wicked,
like the heat that creates optical illusions for blind men in oil-lamps.
Even a very small [deed] of the virtuous remains like an inscription on stone;
that of the base remains like a line drawn on water.
Even that which has been done perishes.
Even a small gift to the virtuous is a support, like water in a well.
Even a multitude of the wicked is not like water in the ocean;
for his mind would be corrupted.
Anger is like a scratch on stone;
whereas for a virtuous person, anger is like a line drawn on water,
which does not last long.
The life of a fool is wretched,
like crossing a river in a boat;
he is like a king to the multitude of people.
The duty of kings is like that of kings;
the powerful lion is like those with fangs,
while the ant is like the eater of crumbs.
Then the king Narā was powerful;
the slayer of all was powerful.
The earth, water, fire, woman, and the craftsman—
A person who is covetous;
even among these who have great desire,
their state of great desiring is impermanent.
One who is drowsy, discontented,
ungrateful, and cowardly—
such a person is unable to practice right conduct.
To train themselves, they will never have the opportunity—
those who are sleepy, delighting in sensual pleasures,
happy, and addicted to wealth.
The one who desires nothing, the one who delights in work—
these seven, excluding the Teacher,
were Samiddha, rich in wealth and grain.
A piece of wood is consumed by fire from dung or grass;
one who is destitute is ruined on all sides.
Therefore, do not commit evil deeds.
He who does not truly believe in the fruit of merit and evil will indeed quickly [destroy] himself.
One should bring forth the surface of a mirror.
Even if one does not have faith in the goal pertaining to future lives, [one should still do so].
In this dwelling, what does he not see belonging to those bound for heaven—
such as great round trees and the like?
Having witnessed for oneself that even a tiny seed yields abundant fruit,
a person who performs both merit and evil should look ahead with discernment.
For one who makes light of respect and honor, those very things become light for them.
The attainment of the perfection of true knowledge;
and [the service] toward preceptors and teachers,
as well as toward one's mother and father.
He attends carefully and with proper mindfulness;
his father was likewise learned.
And in various places, among the families...
One should visit that country where there are such kinsmen born together with one.
One should admonish a wicked son or brother,
but one should not abandon them;
for what is the point of cutting off a foot that is doing harm?
It may be smeared with impurity;
though he has many sons,
the father alone must always support them.
Though they have many sons,
they are not able to support their father alone;
whether he is of higher birth or of equal birth—
The wise desire sons who bring honor;
they do not desire one who is base-born,
who brings disgrace upon the family.
Seeing five advantages,
the wise desire a son:
"He will support us when he is born,"...
He will perform his duty for us;
the family lineage will endure for long,
and the inheritance will be maintained.
Or else, he will provide an offering for the departed spirits;
though born within [the household],
he was bought with wealth.
One who has entered into servitude by oneself,
one brought there as a slave by others,
and likewise those born as slaves— thus there would be four kinds of slaves.
The five kinds of slaves— those who are like thieves,
those who are like friends, and those who are like kinsmen—
are to be understood by the wise in this way.
One's wife and kinsmen are one's companions;
these three alone are one's true teachers,
and I am the one who speaks beyond them.
One who says "I am" and one who says "I am not"—
these two would not go without a teacher.
A hero on the field of battle,
a wise traveler, a merchant,
and likewise one who journeys to foreign lands.
Having investigated thoroughly both the syllables and the meanings,
a student may become a slayer of thieves.
The teacher is a thief and a wrongdoer.
Goodness in the wicked arises from association with the virtuous;
in the virtuous, wickedness arises from association with the wicked.
The earth bears the fragrance arising from the flowers,
yet the flowers do not possess the scent of the earth. Likewise,
one should not associate with a friend who is base, nor with a teaching that is defiled.
Those who desire success through the suffering of others,
knowledge through ease, and a wife through harshness,
are indeed no wise men at all.
Having performed wholesome deeds in conversation with friends,
and having performed unwholesome deeds in the past;
They share in both happiness and suffering;
he who does not see this is a fool,
[afflicted] by the evil he has done himself.
One receives an undesired fruit;
yet the fool thinks, "They gave birth to him for me," and thus performs evil deeds once again.
Through the passage of time,
the dull-witted person neglects generosity, virtue,
and the like; he considers even what is unstable to be stable.
Like a fool who,
having committed an evil deed,
attempts to hide his own self as if it were eternal.
How could one who is fleeing from a tiger or such dangers dare to smear his footprints?
He is lost through his flight from others.
Just as a fire that consumes its fuel quickly reaches the sight [of the observer],
so too does one who burns down a palace [with straw] reach the sight [of the king].
Eating, sexual intercourse, sleep,
and the tending of cattle exist [even for animals];
but the distinguishing mark of a person is wisdom.
Therefore, one who is deficient becomes like an ox:
because of his deluded students and because of supporting a barren wife.
Through association with wicked enemies, even a wise person comes to grief.
These two are sharp thorns: [the one who does not give when asked and the one who asks when there is nothing to give].
Those who beautify their bodies with sensual pleasures,
who seek after desires, and who are undisciplined and lack renunciation— [they are lost].
One who hoards wealth desires sensual pleasures;
one who is weak delights in quarreling;
one with dull wisdom has a dispute as his aim.
There are three characteristics of delusion:
A person of little learning, though possessing little learning,
considers himself to be great in wisdom.
Observing the water of the Sindhu river,
like a frog in a well;
by this too one may know.
Hearing the sounds from the springs and the cracks,
the kusumbha fish depart;
the great ocean remains silent.
Whatever is deficient, that he hears;
whatever is full, that remains as it is.
The fool is like a half-filled jar.
A wise man is like a full lake;
even when speaking,
a fool possesses many pretenses.
An ember being crushed does not turn blue; likewise,
beauty [is no match] for another's wife.
Wealth is for the satisfaction of the world;
it is devoted to the nose of the virtuous,
yet in the wicked, its qualities become even more base.
There is nothing in this world more laughable than that which they call "a wicked person."
The wicked man himself is a thorn to the good man,
a sprout of disease, a fire,
and a dense cloud of discord.
Peace is not found through non-destruction, nor indeed through dependence on others;
it is not found through the doctrines of others.
The wicked indeed take delight [in excrement];
having tasted all flavors,
they do not grow weary of it without excrement.
When struck, it joins back together;
when cut, it becomes a forest.
What can be done with the soft heart of an evil person?
It is compared to iron.
Therefore, one should avoid association with the wicked,
as one would a venomous serpent.
One who desires prosperity and possesses discernment should avoid them from afar;
for association with the wicked—
Even being hot is not appropriate; therefore, the ember burns,
while that which is cool brings about the end of time.
An evil person is to be avoided,
even if adorned with knowledge;
just as a virtuous person is not to be shunned, even if adorned with a jewel.
Is a serpent not terrifying?
Yet when the fire burns the forest,
the wind becomes its friend.
He destroys even his own island;
when a rogue is gone, there is no longer friendship.
One does not grieve for one who has committed evil.
One should not despise a speaker of falsehood;
one should not despise one whose wisdom is directed toward the goal;
nor should one despise one who speaks excessively.
How many wicked people, who are like the sky, can one possibly kill?
They are killed by an angry mind.
The wicked have been slain;
the ground is strewn with thorns that cannot even be covered over.
With only a pair of sandals,
the earth is covered;
beings always frequent [only] what is near.
Whether it be water, ponds,
and so forth, or even enjoyments and wealth—
if these are empty, they abandon them.
A friend may abandon one who is destitute of wealth—
sons, wife, and brothers alike—
but those possessing wealth are served by all.
In this world, purpose is the great companion.
It is neither material form nor wisdom;
it is the striving of one of noble lineage.
In times of both misfortune and prosperity,
it is the virtuous friend who is the true wealth and the guide through the wilderness.
They wish to speak in the assembly as if in battle;
these four people are deluded and seek to go where they do not belong.
The prevention of what is harmful,
the application toward what is beneficial,
and the relinquishing of misdeeds.
In brief, the characteristics of a friend are as follows:
when one is afflicted by illness, fallen into calamity,
during a famine, or in the midst of conflict with enemies.
He who stands by one even at the king’s gate or in the cemetery is a true kinsman;
he who is devoted to one's welfare is a kinsman.
He alone is a father who provides support;
he alone is a kinsman in whom one can place trust;
she alone is a wife in whom there is security.
Those who speak kindly, those who act with friendship,
and wise people are rare to find;
likewise, one who is both pleasant and agreeable is hard to encounter.
A good person is a remover of disease;
they are not heavy-laden, nor are they lazy;
they are free from deceit, truthful, and pure.
One who is free from greed and desires welfare—
such a person is the supreme happy one, who, having renounced what is permanent, [seeks] the impermanent.
He cultivates what is impermanent;
even his permanent [attainments] perish,
for he has found no footing among the impermanent.
One should win over the stubborn by means of seizing wealth,
the arrogant by prostrations,
and the deluded by compliance with their desires.
One should overcome a wise man by means of truth as it is;
a superior man by prostrating at his feet;
and a hero by means of strategic division.
One should conquer an inferior person with gifts,
and an equal by valor; for whatever the nature of each may be,
[one should act accordingly].
Therefore, having entered into that man,
the wise one should quickly bring him under his own control.
One should not employ the three negatives with that which one intends to connect;
[this applies to] a connection between a dispute and a matter.
Seeing the wife in her absence,
through excessive and frequent association,
and by not forgetting [her].
By this, friendships wear away,
as does begging at the wrong time.
Therefore, one should not go [to beg] constantly.
One should not go too long without going;
one should make a request at the proper time.
In this way, one does not cause friends to decay.
These go together even more closely;
their bond does not decay—
for he who endures what has come upon him.
And whoever understands the teaching—
if they dispute while remaining calm,
they shall quickly reach reconciliation again.
The foolish break apart even while still together;
they have not attained inner peace.
Through whatever friendship there is association, [they fall away].
The peace of yoga is lost for one who is already burning; therefore,
a wise person should guard what has not yet been cast away.
One should associate with such friends that through their company one's security from bondage increases;
one should conduct oneself in a manner equal to theirs.
In all undertakings, the wise man—
even if his virtues are equal to those of the Omniscient One—
sinks if he lacks support.
This priceless ruby shines by depending on gold;
just as each joint of the sugarcane [shines] in succession.
From the Chapter on the Essence of Excellence:
Likewise, a good friend is virtuous,
while a wicked person is the opposite.
By that very Sage it was said:
"Whatever mundane phenomena there are,
as well as those leading to Nibbāna,"
There are supramundane states.
Having approached a spiritual friend,
all those [states] belong to living beings.
Therefore, one should always show respect toward virtuous friends;
for he who is grateful, mindful of what has been done, and steadfast—
One who is a virtuous friend and firm in devotion,
who carefully attends to the needs of one who is suffering—
such a person they call a true man.
Whatever Dhamma a person should understand,
and by which the virtuous remove his doubt—
that indeed is his island and his refuge.
A wise person’s friendship does not decay because of that. [The types of friends are:
the leader, the counselor, the farmer, the merchant, and the servant.
The ascetic who possesses learning and virtue— when these have increased extensively,
the kingdom too shall become extensive.
If those [officials] are weak, the kingdom too will be weak;
therefore, even a vast kingdom—
The King, the Essence of the Realm, maintains this:
he who plucks the unripe fruit from a great, fruit-bearing tree.
He does not know its sap,
and its seed perishes;
such is a kingdom like a great tree.
He who governs by unrighteousness does not understand the true essence of things,
and the kingdom shall perish.
He who plucks the ripe fruit from a great tree laden with fruit experiences its flavor as well.
He does not even remember its seed.
A kingdom that one rules according to the Dhamma is like a great tree.
The king perceives the flavor [of the land],
yet he does not forget the kingdom;
and whatever the realm of people may be, [he knows it].
He who rules by unrighteousness,
that king along with all his allies,
becomes an enemy to the kṣatriya class.
Likewise, those engaged in buying and selling, in the collection of taxes, and in the offering of oblations,
commit violence within the marketplace.
He is obstructed by his own storehouse.
In the great fields of Rāvara,
Saṅga, I have performed my service.
For a king who, though exalted,
commits violence, is struck down by his own army;
even so is the sage who commits violence.
The one who practices celibacy with self-restraint,
while the Khattiya acts contrary to the Dhamma,
is obstructed from the heavenly realm.
Not made by oneself, nor by another,
nor fashioned by a great lord;
likewise not by Īśvara, nor by a king.
Sovereignty over the country;
for whether it be evil or merit,
he who exerts himself performs it.
The world indeed acts in this way;
a wise person should understand that.
[It is the same] for female tortoises and female fish.
Just as hens and cows are nurturers of their young,
so too are kings toward men.
Those without a leader perish;
those with many leaders perish;
those led by women perish.
Many leaders lead them away,
all of whom imagine themselves to be wise.
All desire greatness, yet what they have done perishes;
it leads only to their downfall and destruction.
Having many leaders is a source of ruin;
lotuses withered by low-born beings do not bloom, but perish.
The ascetic who is discontented is lost;
the king who is contented is a lord of the earth;
the courtesan who has a sense of shame is lost.
A woman of noble family is not shameless.
One should not go away from the group;
when the task is accomplished, the fruit is shared equally.
If there is a failure in the ritual,
the talkative one is struck down therein;
and so too is the stubborn ascetic.
Sūra, Raṇavaṇa, likewise Majjapa,
Patithī, and Rājā—
I do not believe in these.
One should know a servant by his execution of orders,
kinsmen when danger has arrived,
and likewise a friend in times of misfortune.
A wife when wealth is exhausted,
a hero returned from battle,
and wealth that has come back home.
One should praise an old man,
and a wife whose youth has passed,
as long as faith and love still remain.
A hundred māsakas given to a group of the faithless is as nothing;
but when there are those possessed of faith,
even a single māsaka given to such a group is a hundredfold.
The gift that tames the untamed,
the gift that accomplishes all aims; through giving and through pleasant speech, [one gains a companion].
They rise up and they bend down:
generosity is the medicine for affection,
while stinginess is the medicine for ill-will.
Generosity is the medicine for fame,
stinginess is the medicine for poverty;
and giving food during a famine—
Giving food during a famine, giving gold,
and giving safety in times of fear—
these are highly esteemed even in heaven.
The disciples of the Leader always possess the eye of wisdom and the ear of wisdom;
nevertheless, he remains steadfast even toward the blind.
This is the nature of a leader:
forbearance, wakefulness,
steadfastness, sharing, and compassion.
These are the qualities of a leader that one who desires their own welfare should seek.
When treated with contempt, he remains gentle.
Excessive severity brings enmity;
having understood both of these,
one should practice with moderation.
It is not possible to establish the self in greatness by means of that which is exclusively soft, nor by that which is exclusively sharp.
Therefore, one should practice both:
one should attend to the fire at one's back,
and the sacrificial fire within the belly.
One should serve one's husband with one's whole being,
and the next world with sincerity;
one should not serve a harsh husband.
One should avoid that person who is stingy;
then one should associate with one who encourages [virtue], and after that, with one who restrains [faults].
He is no king who conquers one who cannot be conquered;
he is no friend who overcomes his friend;
she is no wife who opposes her husband.
They are not called [true] monks who do not honor their elders.
That is no assembly where the virtuous do not sit.
They are not virtuous who do not speak according to the Dhamma.
Having abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion,
the virtuous ones indeed speak the Dhamma;
constant application is the protection of what has been heard.
The duty of a family, the learning of a man,
the negligence of a king, and the wealth of one who is tranquil—
I know these, but I never know the protection of women.
A wise man [should avoid] talk concerning women, whether it be with his mother, his daughter, or his sister.
One should not dwell in a secluded seat,
nor with deceitful women,
nor amidst the flickering instability of lightning.
Women imitate the sharpness of weapons, and the swiftness of wind and fire.
Sloth and food have a twofold effect,
wisdom has a fourfold effect,
and effort has a sixfold effect.
In the arising of eight qualities for each woman,
there would be eight husbands for each wife.
Brave and powerful,
bringing all desired flavors,
one should apply zeal in the ninth [jhāna].
For those who are already full are not filled further;
they prattle along with others while looking elsewhere with flirtatious gestures.
Who indeed would be dear to women when they are thinking of another man?
For even one who possesses a thousand tongues—
Even if a man were to live for a hundred years,
he is said to be devoid of action if he has not reached the destruction of the fault of lust.
Fire, water, women, a fool,
a snake, and royal families—
one should avoid these by all means.
"Taking away the life from Death's grasp":
for women and wicked men,
no confidence arises.
The diseases of the twenty-horned one,
and those of the river and the royal family—
even for one whose mind is well-resolved, these must be reflected upon with a weapon.
Even a king well-served must be suspected;
even a young woman who has come into one's hands must be guarded.
Where, then, can there be security for a young woman on a journey with a teacher?
Conflict arises from undertaking unsuitable work,
as does war with those of great power for the sake of the Saṅgha;
one should always avoid placing trust in those who are negligent.
They say wisdom is the door to the deathless.
A man might grasp the wind with his net,
or pour out the ocean with a single hand.
One who abandons all concern for beings might produce a sound with his mouth and palms; for even among women,
there is indeed one of a certain kind.
The Sage has indeed spoken of the bed;
the woman is the best of possessions,
and she is the supreme attendant.
He who always supports him—
who is ever diligent and zealous,
the provider of all desires— [is truly a supporter].
She does not despise her husband,
nor does she cause her husband distress through jealousy or misconduct.
The wise person honors all their teachers,
rising early and free from indolence.
She keeps her attendants under control;
she acts agreeably to her husband and protects his property.
Thus does the woman on the vehicle proceed,
following the will and desire of her husband;
those gods are indeed called "the agreeable."
Wherever she is reborn,
the cuckoo’s song is her form,
and the beauty of women is her appearance.
Knowledge is the beauty of those with and without form;
forbearance is the beauty of ascetics.
Wisdom is the beauty of one born of noble lineage.
One may arrange a marriage even for an ugly girl with a handsome man of low status,
as if it were a perfect match.
From the wicked comes what is not to be accepted;
from the base comes gold;
even from the lowly comes the highest wisdom.

The setambu fruit and betel leaf do not become defiled by remnants;
nor does the *bālakka* leaf or its smoke.
Women who have grown old, water from a stagnant pool,
that which constantly causes the exhaustion of life,
and eating curd at night.
One should serve women who dance,
eat what is delicious though it be unwholesome,
and honor and respect the elders.
One should not honor a teacher through deceit.
Conduct reveals one's lineage;
speech reveals one's country.
Sambhava explains "love," while *deha* explains "food.
Through the word *dehī*,
[the meaning is established].
The five deities residing in the body—
Modesty, Renown, Wisdom, Shame, and Glory— are always present.
The statement "there is a body" is suffering,
and likewise the statement "there is no [body]";
the expressions "there is a body" and "there is no [body]"—
May there be no further existence in birth after birth.
People awaken [to this truth] and entreat [the donor], saying,
"Give!"— thus do the people of later times speak.
Behold the gift of a cloth;
let it not be like this.
A great thing passes away for the sake of a trifle.
Even one possessed of virtues here among those devoid of virtue,
by virtue of being worthy of offerings,
is like a lordly elephant amidst mere brushwood.
By relying on something great,
even a small thing may become very large;
just as by reaching the mountain of gold.
Even golden-winged birds [cannot overcome] the combined strength of many, however weak they may be;
for unity is indeed difficult to conquer.
With grass one can make a rope,
and with that even a nāga is bound; thus,
even one who is capable is powerless if he is without a companion.
What will his brilliance accomplish?
Like a fire standing in a windless place,
it will extinguish itself.
The heat and brilliance of fire can be endured,
but not that which arises from praise;
punishment inflicted by kings and others [is likewise unbearable].
One who eats fish is not free from fear;
how can one purified by association with women be pure?
How can there be true prosperity for one who eats meat?
In one who drinks liquor, whence can there be truth?
In one who is corrupt, whence can there be austerity?
One should not disclose the secret of a woman.
The wise man who is not intimate with a foe,
and the steadfast man who is intimate with both—
such a person has his heart as his shield.
The man who awakens the secret meaning out of fear of the disclosure of his counsel—
He endures like a slave,
carrying the burden of his enemies as long as the time has not yet come.
And at that very time, he broke the jar, the lily,
the threshing floor, the sal tree, the cattle, and the field.
Having gone [to the field], he should frequently sow the grain in measured amounts,
and he should have it harvested in measured amounts at home.
Anger, greed, intoxication, pride, sloth,
negligence, arrogance, indolence, and hypocrisy.
The wise one should abandon stinginess.
Anger born within destroys the angry person, just as incense consumes itself.
If anger should arise, it is like a peacock entering a basket filled with garments and ornaments.
One should reflect on the simile of the saw;
if craving for flavors should arise,
one should remember the simile of the son’s flesh.
When there is a quarrel with another, one should smear oneself with virtues that surpass them;
one should manifest virtues that exceed theirs.
Even a tiny fault is worse for that person who,
being angry, returns anger for anger.
Not retaliating against one who is angry,
he conquers a battle difficult to win.
Passion, indeed, is the arrow of the mind.
The fulfiller of the highest purpose through his virtues;
the one who consumes the sacrificial fire of asceticism, like Rāhu to the moon of knowledge.
From intoxication arises negligence;
from negligence arises ruin;
from ruin arise corruptions.
What intoxication would the wise man not abandon?
Fruit-bearing trees bend low,
and likewise do those who are awakened.
Like dry wood and one who is deluded,
their knowledge breaks apart;
there is no room for the elders in that situation.
He gave it away, being one who honors his elders;
for does not even a palmyra tree,
though lifeless, bend down when another is near?
He who maintains constant conduct toward those who are worthy of honor,
having abandoned negligence, [attains the goal].
One is established in the highest state,
where people do not recognize one by birth or by discipline.
One should not take pride there;
dwell among people who do not know you.
Dwell as one who is unknown.
Even if one is threatened by a servant,
a wise person should endure it as if from one equal to Jātavedas.
In the management of wealth and grain,
as well as in the acquisition of various sciences,
in the role of a messenger, and in legal transactions—
One should always be free from shame;
for when a deed has been done,
no one looks closely at the doer.
Therefore, one should have all tasks performed with something remaining;
a remainder of debt is like a remainder of fire.
There are these three remaining factors;
they increase again and again.
Therefore, one should not allow anything else to remain.
There is no wealth equal to knowledge,
no enemy equal to disease,
and no love equal to oneself.
There is no power superior to karma.
One creates fortune for oneself,
and misfortune as well, by oneself.
Neither luck nor ill fortune brings about one another's result; rather,
it is by oneself that one's own prosperity and decline are brought about by the king.
One should know for oneself what has been done and what has not been done;
by oneself alone one must experience the results of both what was done and what was left undone.
One should extract an enemy with one's own hand, as if helping him with a benefit,
even when that enemy has stepped upon one's foot.
One should meet thorn with thorn;
one should associate with the bowing person who bows,
and one should perform for the doer what is to be done.
One should not do what is beneficial for one who has no desire for it,
nor should one associate with one who does not associate.
One should abandon one who abandons, but should not act toward them as one who is ungrateful.
One should not associate with one whose mind has departed [from virtue],
just as a bird, perceiving a tree to be devoid of fruit,
would look toward another; for the world is full of great things.
